claims.text: Design involves the enacting of theory through the body; design is 'doing philosophy with the hands'.
Philosophy is one of the least-discussed fields shaping experience design, despite extensive work on psychology, cognitive science, and anthropology.
In the U.S., academics and practitioners are mostly closed off from one another despite the crossover in their work; phenomenology can bridge the gap by treating theory and practice as one system.
Phenomenology emphasizes praxis as a means of knowledge, so an academic-toned book can still be practice-oriented; this is not a recipe book.
We have developed products well but designed them badly; the pendulum has swung too far from thinking to making, yielding products that lack utility or meaningful interaction.

Startup/VC economies have fetishized the launch, producing products that are polished but not architected, beautiful but useless, conceptually unique but aesthetically templated, commercially viable but morally corrupt.
The obsessive need to launch and iterate ironically links design to phenomenology, since testing with users is itself a phenomenological concern.
Lean Startup and Lean UX rightly emphasize customer insight but are easily bastardized into biased methods that reinforce shallow assumptions.
Treating problems and solutions as a linear movement creates a false assumption about where to start; problems and solutions co-evolve (the problem-solution paradox).

Phenomenology's next evolution is design-centric: if technology is how we understand the world, how we design technology is massively important, and one cannot discuss technology without discussing design.
Cross's definition of design phenomenology is too narrow and in fact encompasses design praxiology and design epistemology, because artifacts embody our understanding of the world.
There is no word for 'design' in classical Greek or Hebrew; design is peculiarly modern, indicative of a modern way of being-in-the-world (Mitcham).

Craft lacks separation between maker and user; design is the purposeful enacting of an intentional plan under a complex system of influences (industry standards, market viability, user behavior, feasibility).
We cannot dictate experience (it is purely personal and varies across individuals) but can design for the potential of certain qualitative experiences over others.
The designer-user rift means experience design is fickle and best understood as the emergent effect of many design practices, hence multi- and trans-disciplinary.
Heidegger's German-rooted complexity makes phenomenological terminology hard; Wendt will stay consistent with popular translations and explain when needed.
Designers have become too reliant on case studies, recipe books, and step-by-step guides; strong frameworks offer more value than accounts of single instances, so this book omits case studies.
